RESUMO

O

jet

lag

social

(SJL),

definido

como

o

desalinhamento

entre

os

horários

biológicos

e

as

demandas

sociais,

tem

sido

reconhecido

como

um

fenômeno

altamente

prevalente

na

adolescência,

período

marcado

por

profundas

transformações

biológicas,

comportamentais

e

psicossociais.

Esta

tese

teve

como

objetivo

investigar

a

associação

entre

o

SJL

e

desfechos

cardiometabólicos,

comportamentais

e

de

bem-estar

em

adolescentes

brasileiros,

bem

como

analisar

sua

distribuição

epidemiológica

e

implicações

para

políticas

públicas

em

saúde

e

educação.

O

trabalho

é

composto

por

dois

artigos

científicos

complementares.

O

primeiro,

de

base

populacional,

estimou

a

prevalência

de

SJL

e

avaliou

sua

associação

com

indicadores

antropométricos,

perfil

cardiometabólico

e

comportamentos

relacionados

à

saúde,

evidenciando

que

maiores

discrepâncias

entre

os

horários

de

sono

em

dias

úteis

e

fins

de

semana

estiveram

associadas

a

piores

indicadores

de

adiposidade

e

maior

exposição

a

comportamentos

de

risco,

independentemente

da

duração

total

do

sono.

O

segundo

artigo

aprofundou

a

análise

ao

examinar

desfechos

funcionais

e

de

bem-estar,

incluindo

aptidão

cardiorrespiratória,

padrões

de

atividade

física,

alimentação

e

indicadores

emocionais,

reforçando

o

papel

do

SJL

como

um

estressor

fisiológico

e

comportamental

independente.

Adicionalmente,

a

ampla

repercussão

dos

resultados

em

meios

de

comunicação

evidenciou

o

interesse

social

pelo

tema

e

fomentou

debates

públicos

sobre

horários

escolares,

uso

de

dispositivos

eletrônicos

e

organização

da

rotina

adolescente.

Os

achados

desta

tese

contribuem

para

a

literatura

ao

consolidar

o

SJL

como

um

marcador

relevante

de

vulnerabilidade

cardiometabólica

na

adolescência

e

ao

destacar

a

necessidade

de

estratégias

intersetoriais

que

integrem

saúde

e

educação.

Por

fim,

o

trabalho

dialoga

com

diretrizes

da

pós-graduação

brasileira

ao

evidenciar

a

produção

científica,

formativa

e

de

inserção

social

desenvolvida

durante

o

doutorado,

realizado

em

contexto

semipresencial

e

de

atuação

docente

em

universidade

federal,

reforçando

o

papel

da

pós-graduação

na

geração

de

conhecimento

socialmente

relevante

e

na

formulação

de

políticas

públicas

baseadas

em

evidências.

ABSTRACT

Social

jet

lag

(SJL),

defined

as

the

misalignment

between

biological

timing

and

socially

imposed

schedules,

has

emerged

as

a

highly

prevalent

phenomenon

during

adolescence,

a

life

stage

characterized

by

intense

biological,

behavioral,

and

psychosocial

changes.

This

doctoral

thesis

aimed

to

investigate

the

association

between

SJL

and

cardiometabolic,

behavioral,

and

well-being

outcomes

in

Brazilian

adolescents,

as

well

as

to

examine

its

epidemiological

distribution

and

implications

for

public

health

and

educational

policies.

The

thesis

comprises

two

complementary

scientific

articles.

First,

a

population-based

study

estimated

the

prevalence

of

SJL

and

assessed

its

association

with

anthropometric

indicators,

cardiometabolic

risk

factors,

and

health-related

behaviors,

demonstrating

that

greater

discrepancies

between

weekday

and

weekend

sleep

timing

were

associated

with

poorer

adiposity

indicators

and

increased

exposure

to

risk

behaviors,

independent

of

total

sleep

duration.

The

second

article

extended

these

findings

by

examining

functional

and

well-being

outcomes,

including

cardiorespiratory

fitness,

physical

activity

patterns,

dietary

behaviors,

and

emotional

indicators,

reinforcing

the

role

of

SJL

as

an

independent

physiological

and

behavioral

stressor.

Furthermore,

the

broad

dissemination

of

the

findings

through

mass

media

highlighted

the

social

relevance

of

the

topic

and

stimulated

public

debate

on

school

starting

times,

electronic

device

use,

and

adolescent

daily

routines.

Overall,

the

results

contribute

to

the

literature

by

consolidating

SJL

as

a

relevant

marker

of

cardiometabolic

vulnerability

during

adolescence

and

by

emphasizing

the

need

for

intersectoral

strategies

integrating

health

and

education.

Finally,

the

thesis

aligns

with

Brazilian

graduate

education

guidelines

by

highlighting

the

scientific

output,

training

activities,

and

social

engagement

developed

during

the

doctoral

program,

conducted

in

a

hybrid

format

alongside

faculty

appointment

at

a

federal

university,

underscoring

the

role

of

graduate

education

in

producing

socially

relevant,

evidence-based

knowledge.

INTRODUÇÃO


Os

padrões

individuais

de

sono

são

regulados

pelas

complexas

interações

entre

fatores

biológicos

(como

sexo

e

idade),

genéticos,

ambientais

(como

a

exposição

à

luz)

e

comportamentais

(Wong

et

al.
,

2015).

Esses

fatores

influenciam

a

organização

temporal

do

sono

por

meio

do

sistema

circadiano,

também

chamado

de

ritmo

biológico,

responsável

por

sincronizar

processos

os

fisiológicos

ao

longo

das

24

horas

diárias.

Quando

esse

ritmo

entra

em

conflito

com

as

demandas

e

horários

sociais,

podem

ocorrer

situações

de

desalinhamento,

que

se

manifestam,

entre

outras

formas,

pelo

fenômeno

conhecido

como

jet

lag

social

(SJL)

(Roenneberg

et

al.
,

2012).


Do

ponto

de

vista

epidemiológico,

observam-se

que

as

distribuições

de

padrão

de

sono,

apresentam

variação

heterogênea

na

população,

segundo

sexo,

faixa

etária

e

contexto

sociocultural,

com

tendência

ao

atraso

de

fase

durante

a

adolescência

(Karan

et

al.
,

2021;

Thomas

C,

Peter

e

Philip,

2025).

Esse

deslocamento

fisiológico

do

ritmo

circadiano,

quando

confrontado

com

horários

sociais

rígidos,

como

horários

escolares,

aumenta

a

vulnerabilidade

ao

desalinhamento

circadiano

nessa

faixa

etária

(Jankovic

et

al.
,

2022).

O

conceito

de

SJL

foi

proposto

por

Wittmann

et

al.

(2006)

e

refere-se

à

discrepância

entre

o

ritmo

circadiano

individual

e

os

horários

impostos

por

obrigações

sociais,

como

escola

ou

trabalho.

Esse

desalinhamento

pode

comprometer

a

duração

e

a

qualidade

do

sono

durante

a

semana,

levando

à

compensação

com

maior

tempo

de

sono

nos

finais

de

semana

e,

consequentemente,

à

variação

no

ponto

médio

do

sono.

Operacionalmente,

o

SJL

é

calculado

como

a

diferença

absoluta

entre

o

ponto

médio

do

sono

nos

finais

de

semana

(MSF)

e

nos

dias

de

semana

(MSW)

(Wittmann

et

al.,2006).


Evidências

recentes

indicam

que

o

desalinhamento

circadiano,

expresso

pelo

SJL,

pode

estar

associado

a

desfechos

cardiometabólicos

em

populações

jovens.

Em

estudo

transversal

conduzido

com

847

adolescentes

espanhóis

de

12

a

17

anos,

Mayra

Fernanda

Martínez-López

e

José

Francisco

López-Gil

observaram

que

maiores

níveis

de

SJL

estiveram

significativamente

associados

a

maiores

valores

de

IMC-z,

circunferência

da

cintura

e

percentual

de

gordura

corporal,

além

de

maior

probabilidade

de

excesso

de

peso,

obesidade

e

obesidade

abdominal

(Martínez-López

&

López-Gil,

2024).

Nesse

contexto,

o

SJL

tem

sido

apontado

como

um

potencial

marcador

de

risco

no

campo

da

saúde

pública,

especialmente

no

cenário

das

Doenças

Crônicas

Não

Transmissíveis

(DCNT).

Considerando

esse

cenário,

é

fundamental

investigar

a

prevalência

de

SJL

entre

adolescentes

brasileiros,

bem

como

sua

relação

com

fatores

comportamentais

e

11

sociodemográficos,

além

da

possível

associação

com

alterações

em

indicadores

cardiometabólicos

de

saúde

nessa

fase

da

vida.

ABSTRACT


Objectives:

Social

jetlag

is

a

disturbance

in

the

circadian

rhythm

caused

by

a

desynchronization

between

an

individual’s

biological

rhythm

and

social

commitments

and

responsibilities.

It

leads

to

sleep

debt

during

the

week

and

compensation

on

weekends.

Social

jetlag

is

associated

with

an

increased

risk

of

chronic

diseases

and

cognitive

dysfunction

in

adolescents.

This

study

aims

to

assess

the

prevalence

of

social

jetlag

and

associated

factors

in

Brazilian

adolescents.

Methods:

Adolescents

of

both

sexes,

aged

between

12

and

17

years,

participating

in

the

Study

of

Cardiovascular

Risks

in

Adolescents

(ERICA),

were

included.

The

sleep

duration

on

a

typical

weekday

and

weekend

day

was

collected

through

a

self-reported

questionnaire.

The

occurrence

of

social

jetlag

was

defined

as

the

difference

between

the

midpoint

of

sleep

on

weekends

and

weekdays,

with

differences

equal

to

or

higher

than

1

hour

considered

as

an

indicator

of

positive

social

jetlag.

Factors

associated

with

the

prevalence

of

social

jetlag

were

investigated

using

Poisson

regression

models.

Results:

The

sample

included

a

total

of

64,029

adolescents.

Social

jetlag

affects

more

than

80%

of

Brazilian

adolescents,

with

higher

prevalence

among

girls

in

the

age

group

of

16-17

years,

with

white

skin

color,

attending

private

schools,

and

those

having

morning

classes.

Additionally,

unhealthy

risk

behaviors

such

as

skipping

breakfast,

alcohol

consumption,

and

increased

screen

time

are

associated

with

a

higher

prevalence

of

social

jetlag.

Conclusion:

The

prevalence

of

social

jetlag

was

high

in

Brazilian

adolescents,

and,

among

its

associated

factors,

studying

in

the

morning

shift

and

engaging

in

unhealthy

risk

behaviors

stand

out.

Keywords:

Social

jetlag,

Circadian

rhythm,

Sleep,

Epidemiological

studies

41


I
ntroduction


The

circadian

rhythm,

an

individual

biological

rhythmic

pattern,

is

susceptible

to

influences

of

biological,

genetic,

environmental,

and

behavioral

nature.
1

Changes

in

this

rhythmic

pattern

result

in

a

desynchronization

between

internal

and

external

time,

referred

to

as

social

jetlag

(SJL),

indicating

the

misalignment

of

the

biological

rhythm

caused

by

social

commitments

and

responsibilities.
1

In

adolescents,

SJL

is

more

pronounced

than

in

any

other

age

group,

primarily

due

to

bioregulatory

sleep

pressures

that

increase

nocturnal

arousal,

consequently

leading

to

a

delayed

sleep

phase.
2

Although

there

is

no

evidence

to

state

that

physiological

changes

(e.g.,

dim

light

melatonin

onset

phase)

contribute

to

phase

delay

in

mature

adolescents,
3

social

factors

play

a

significant

role.

These

include

reduced

parental

enforcement

of

bedtimes,

early

school

start

times,

academic

demands,

and

the

use

of

social

networks,

which

enhance

cognitive

arousal.

These

factors

collectively

contribute

to

the

accumulation

of

sleep

debt

during

the

week.
2

As

a

result,

adolescents

often

engage

in

weekend

catch-up

sleep

to

compensate

for

the

sleep

deficit

accrued

during

the

weekdays.
3,4

Additionally,

the

occurrence

of

SJL

in

this

age

group

is

associated

with

psychiatric

alterations,
5

increased

daytime

sleepiness,
6

shorter

sleep

duration,
7

and

cognitive

modifications

in

attention,

memory,

and

executive

function.
8,9

It

is

also

associated

with

an

alteration

in

body

mass

index

and

waist

circumference.
10,11

In

adults,

the

prevalence

of

SJL

of

at

least

1

hour

can

vary

from

70%

among

workers

and

students

to

30%

in

the

general

population.
12

In

adolescents,

the

prevalence

of

SJL

can

vary

by

country.

Among

Chinese

students,

17.8%

experienced

SJL,

considering

two

or

more

hours

as

the

cut-off

point.
13

However,

more

than

half

of

US

adolescents

reported

SJL

before

the

COVID-19

pandemic.
14

Among

Japanese

youth,

the

prevalence

of

SJL

is

also

higher

than

50%

when

using

1

hour

or

more

as

a

cut-off

point.
15

In

Brazil,

few

studies

have

investigated

the

prevalence

of

SJL,

most

of

them

focusing

Study

design

and

sampling

42

study

both

between

12

and

17.

2013

and

Discussion


The

present

study

aimed

to

assess

the

prevalence

of

SJL

among

adolescents,

exploring

the

factors

associated

with

this

condition.

Notably,

this

research

represents

the

first

comprehensive

study,

with

national

representativeness,

on

the

prevalence

of

SJL

and

its

asso-

ciated

factors

among

adolescents

in

Brazil.

The

results

showed

a

high

prevalence

of

SJL,

affecting

more

than

80%

of

adolescents

in

the

country.

SJL

is

more

prevalent

in

female

adolescents,

older

in-

dividuals

(aged

16

to

17

years)

with

self-reported

white

skin

color,

attendees

of

private

schools,

and

with

a

higher

socioeconomic

level.

Moreover,

a

heightened

prevalence

of

SJL

is

linked

to

students

who

attend

morning

classes

and

those

who

engage

in

unhealthy

risk

behaviors,

including

skipping

breakfast,

alcohol

consumption,

and

extended

screen

time.

The

observed

prevalence

of

SJL

was

either

higher

or

similar

to

that

reported

in

other

non-Brazilian

studies.
36,37

In

the

Family

Life,

Activity,

Sun,

Health,

and

Eating

(FLASHE)

47

study,
36

which

involved

adolescents

from

all

regions

of

the

US,

observed

a

prevalence

of

SJL

of

83.2%,

with

higher

rates

among

girls

and

older

adolescents.

Moreover,

aligning

with

our

results,

Jankovic

et

al
37

noted

a

rise

in

SJL

prevalence

with

the

advancing

age

of

German

adolescents.

This

pattern

may

be

attributed

to

physical

maturation

and

the

transition

to

early

adulthood,

characterized

by

a

prolonged

wakefulness

period,

delayed

bedtime,

and

reduced

sleep

time/duration.
2

During

adolescence,

changes

are

observed

in

the

sleep/wake

homeostatic

process

mechanisms,

which

decrease,

especially

among

older

adolescents.

There

is

also

an

influence

on

the

intrinsic

rhythmic

system,

resulting

in

a

delayed

of

and,

consequently,

creating

a

greater

demand

to

wake

up

later

in

the

morning.

The

of

the

(66.8%),

or

in

in

the

morning

does

not

appear

to

prompt

adolescents

to

go

to

bed

earlier,

indicating

no

compensation

in

sleep

time

despite

the

restriction

imposed

by

classes.
38

Others

suggest

that

delaying

the

start

time

of

classes

in

this

age

group

would

increase

sleep

time,

potentially

bringing

health

benefits

and

improving

academic

performance.
36

According

to

Carrell

et

al,
39

starting

the

school

day

50

minutes

later

significantly

improves

student

achievement,

yielding

benefits

comparable

to

an

increase

in

teacher

quality.

Finally,

estimates

from

the

US

working

population

(ages

18-65)

indicate

that

circadian

misalignment

increases

healthcare

costs

by

at

least

2.3

billion

dollars

per

year

due

to

its

association

with

obesity,

diabetes,

and

cardiovascular

diseases.

Additionally,

it

can

lead

to

significant

productivity

losses.

This

highlights

how

work

schedules

and

school

start

times

can

exacerbate

the

detrimental

effects

of

circadian

rhythm

disruptions,

underscoring

the

importance

of

debating

normative

social

schedules.
40

Although

there

is

no

consensus

on

the

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

girls,

some

studies

suggest

that

girls

may

be

more

susceptible

to

the

harmful

effects

of

circadian

rhythm

misalignment.
41

This

susceptibility

may

manifest

in

increased

abdominal

fat,
36

dysregulation

of

hormones

related

to

hunger

and

satiety,
42

and

increased

insulin

resistance,

particularly

in

the

presence

of

polycystic

ovary

syndrome.
43

Regarding

skin

color,

our

results

demonstrated

a

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

adolescents

of

white

skin

color,

which

differs

from

the

study

by

Mezick

et

al,
44

who

identified

a

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

individuals

with

black

or

brown

skin

color.

This

discrepancy

may

be

attributed

to

a

greater

number

of

adolescents

identifying

themselves

as

having

white

skin

in

our

study.

Additionally,

it

is

important

to

consider

that

socioeconomic

and

environmental

characteristics

may

vary

among

different

ethnic

groups,

thereby

influencing

48

sleep

patterns

in

a

complex

manner.
45

One

associated

factor

in

another

study

was

room

temperature

variation,

which

can

impact

sleep

patterns.

In

this

study,

when

the

air

temperature

was

kept

at

a

lower

value

(25°C),

participants

experienced

colder

hands

and

feet

during

the

initial

phase

of

sleep

and

took

a

longer

time

to

fall

asleep,

consequently

reporting

poorer

sleep

quality.
46

We

observe

that

socioeconomic

factors

linked

to

higher

income

are

associated

with

a

greater

prevalence

of

SJL,

in

contrast

to

most

studies

suggesting

that

a

poorer

socioeconomic

condition

is

associated

with

a

higher

prevalence

of

sleep-related

disorders.
15

Ad-

ditionally,

a

lower

prevalence

of

SJL

was

observed

in

the

less

developed

regions

of

the

country

(North

and

Northeast).

Conversely,

regions

with

higher

economic

development

and

urbanization,

such

as

large

cities

in

Southeast

Brazil,

experience

less

exposure

to

sunlight,

more

atmospheric

and

noise

pollution,

and

increased

insecurity,

all

of

which

can

negatively

influence

individuals’

sleep

quality

and

duration.
16,47

These

results

can

also

be

partially

explained

by

geographic

location,

where

individuals

residing

at

northern

latitudes

tend

to

encounter

an

earlier

sunrise,

leading

to

earlier

engagement

in

social

activities

and

adjustments

in

their

morning

routine,
48,49

and

shorter

sleep

compared

with

those

living

in

southern

locations.
50

Further

studies

are

needed

to

investigate

the

role

of

social

and

economic

inequalities

in

adolescents’

sleep

characteristics.

Concerning

unhealthy

risk

behaviors,

adolescents

who

smoked,

drank

alcohol

and

tended

to

skip

breakfast

showed

a

higher

prevalence

of

SJL,

findings

consistent

with

the

literature.
11

Regarding

screen

exposure,

studies

indicate

that

the

use

of

smartphones

or

other

devices

emitting

blue

light,

besides

disrupting

the

sleep

cycle,

may

be

associated

with

the

development

of

cognitive

and

mood

disorders.
5

The

exposure

to

blue

light

emitted

by

screens

can

suppress

the

production

of

melatonin,

a

hormone

related

to

the

light/

dark

cycle,

delaying

the

onset

of

sleep.

It

can

also

affect

body

temperature

regulation

and

individual

perception

of

drowsiness.
51

Furthermore,

greater

cognitive

arousal

created

by

electronic

stimuli

interferes

with

the

production

of

cortisol,

leading

to

sympathetic

hyperstimulation

and

failure

to

regulate

stress.

52

Among

the

limitations

of

our

study

is

the

cross-sectional

research

design,

which

does

not

allow

for

the

establishment

of

a

causal

relationship

between

the

associated

factors

and

SJL.

The

possibility

of

reverse

causality

cannot

be

ruled

out.

The

use

of

questionnaires,

rather

than

objective

data,

to

investigate

sleep

duration

prevented

us

from

obtaining

precise

bedtime

and

wake-up

times

for

adolescents,

as

well

as

the

exact

duration

of

sleep.

The

data

acquired

represents

an

approximation

of

time

spent

in

bed,

and

it

is

prone

to

information

bias.

The

lack

of

standardization

for

the

SJL

cutoff

point

makes

it

difficult

to

compare

studies

regarding

49

prevalence

estimates.

However,

our

study

also

presents

some

strengths.

It

is

a

representative

multicenter

study

of

Brazilian

school-age

adolescents,

with

data

collected

in

a

standardized

manner,

and

the

sleep

duration

was

carefully

checked

for

consistency

in

the

reported

information.

The

large

sample

size

allowed

us

to

analyze

the

prevalence

of

SJL

according

to

different

covariates.

Finally,

the

presented

SJL

prevalence

estimates

provide

novel

information

for

many

regions

in

Brazil.

Conclusion

The

results

of

this

study

are

of

a

high

prevalence

of

SJL

among

Brazilian

school-age

adolescents,

especially

among

older

individuals,

females,

those

of

white

ethnicity,

those

attending

private

schools,

and

those

with

higher

socioeconomic

status.

The

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

students

of

the

morning

shift,

along

with

an

earlier

start

time

for

classes,

suggests

a

potential

partial

sleep

restriction,

indicating

that

modifications

of

school

schedules

could

be

beneficial.

Intervention

studies

to

decrease

the

duration

of

SJL

and

follow-ups

aimed

at

investigating

the

impact

of

SJL

on

health

outcomes

and

academic

performance

are

essential

for

a

comprehensive

understanding

of

their

role

throughout

the

lifespan.

ABSTRACT

Social

jet

lag

(SJL),

defined

as

the

misalignment

between

biological

timing

and

socially

imposed

schedules,

has

emerged

as

a

highly

prevalent

phenomenon

during

adolescence,

a

life

stage

characterized

by

intense

biological,

behavioral,

and

psychosocial

changes.

This

doctoral

thesis

aimed

to

investigate

the

association

between

SJL

and

cardiometabolic,

behavioral,

and

well-being

outcomes

in

Brazilian

adolescents,

as

well

as

to

examine

its

epidemiological

distribution

and

implications

for

public

health

and

educational

policies.

The

thesis

comprises

two

complementary

scientific

articles.

First,

a

population-based

study

estimated

the

prevalence

of

SJL

and

assessed

its

association

with

anthropometric

indicators,

cardiometabolic

risk

factors,

and

health-related

behaviors,

demonstrating

that

greater

discrepancies

between

weekday

and

weekend

sleep

timing

were

associated

with

poorer

adiposity

indicators

and

increased

exposure

to

risk

behaviors,

independent

of

total

sleep

duration.

The

second

article

extended

these

findings

by

examining

functional

and

well-being

outcomes,

including

cardiorespiratory

fitness,

physical

activity

patterns,

dietary

behaviors,

and

emotional

indicators,

reinforcing

the

role

of

SJL

as

an

independent

physiological

and

behavioral

stressor.

Furthermore,

the

broad

dissemination

of

the

findings

through

mass

media

highlighted

the

social

relevance

of

the

topic

and

stimulated

public

debate

on

school

starting

times,

electronic

device

use,

and

adolescent

daily

routines.

Overall,

the

results

contribute

to

the

literature

by

consolidating

SJL

as

a

relevant

marker

of

cardiometabolic

vulnerability

during

adolescence

and

by

emphasizing

the

need

for

intersectoral

strategies

integrating

health

and

education.

Finally,

the

thesis

aligns

with

Brazilian

graduate

education

guidelines

by

highlighting

the

scientific

output,

training

activities,

and

social

engagement

developed

during

the

doctoral

program,

conducted

in

a

hybrid

format

alongside

faculty

appointment

at

a

federal

university,

underscoring

the

role

of

graduate

education

in

producing

socially

relevant,

evidence-based

knowledge.

INTRODUÇÃO


Os

padrões

individuais

de

sono

são

regulados

pelas

complexas

interações

entre

fatores

biológicos

(como

sexo

e

idade),

genéticos,

ambientais

(como

a

exposição

à

luz)

e

comportamentais

(Wong

et

al.
,

2015).

Esses

fatores

influenciam

a

organização

temporal

do

sono

por

meio

do

sistema

circadiano,

também

chamado

de

ritmo

biológico,

responsável

por

sincronizar

processos

os

fisiológicos

ao

longo

das

24

horas

diárias.

Quando

esse

ritmo

entra

em

conflito

com

as

demandas

e

horários

sociais,

podem

ocorrer

situações

de

desalinhamento,

que

se

manifestam,

entre

outras

formas,

pelo

fenômeno

conhecido

como

jet

lag

social

(SJL)

(Roenneberg

et

al.
,

2012).


Do

ponto

de

vista

epidemiológico,

observam-se

que

as

distribuições

de

padrão

de

sono,

apresentam

variação

heterogênea

na

população,

segundo

sexo,

faixa

etária

e

contexto

sociocultural,

com

tendência

ao

atraso

de

fase

durante

a

adolescência

(Karan

et

al.
,

2021;

Thomas

C,

Peter

e

Philip,

2025).

Esse

deslocamento

fisiológico

do

ritmo

circadiano,

quando

confrontado

com

horários

sociais

rígidos,

como

horários

escolares,

aumenta

a

vulnerabilidade

ao

desalinhamento

circadiano

nessa

faixa

etária

(Jankovic

et

al.
,

2022).

O

conceito

de

SJL

foi

proposto

por

Wittmann

et

al.

(2006)

e

refere-se

à

discrepância

entre

o

ritmo

circadiano

individual

e

os

horários

impostos

por

obrigações

sociais,

como

escola

ou

trabalho.

Esse

desalinhamento

pode

comprometer

a

duração

e

a

qualidade

do

sono

durante

a

semana,

levando

à

compensação

com

maior

tempo

de

sono

nos

finais

de

semana

e,

consequentemente,

à

variação

no

ponto

médio

do

sono.

Operacionalmente,

o

SJL

é

calculado

como

a

nesse

torna-se

fundamental

avançar

ABSTRACT


Objectives:

Social

jetlag

is

a

disturbance

in

the

circadian

rhythm

caused

by

a

desynchronization

between

an

individual’s

biological

rhythm

and

social

commitments

and

responsibilities.

It

leads

to

sleep

debt

during

the

week

and

compensation

on

weekends.

Social

jetlag

is

associated

with

an

increased

risk

of

chronic

diseases

and

cognitive

dysfunction

in

adolescents.

This

study

aims

to

assess

the

prevalence

of

social

jetlag

and

associated

factors

in

Brazilian

adolescents.

Methods:

Adolescents

of

both

sexes,

aged

between

12

and

17

years,

participating

in

the

Study

of

Cardiovascular

Risks

in

Adolescents

(ERICA),

were

included.

The

sleep

duration

on

a

typical

weekday

and

weekend

day

was

collected

through

a

self-reported

questionnaire.

The

occurrence

of

social

jetlag

was

defined

as

the

difference

between

the

midpoint

of

sleep

on

weekends

and

weekdays,

with

differences

equal

to

or

higher

than

1

hour

considered

as

an

indicator

of

positive

social

jetlag.

Factors

associated

with

the

prevalence

of

social

jetlag

were

investigated

using

Poisson

regression

models.

Results:

The

sample

included

a

total

of

64,029

adolescents.

Social

jetlag

affects

more

than

80%

of

Brazilian

adolescents,

with

higher

prevalence

among

girls

in

the

age

group

of

16-17

years,

with

white

skin

color,

attending

private

schools,

and

those

having

morning

classes.

Additionally,

unhealthy

risk

behaviors

such

as

skipping

breakfast,

alcohol

consumption,

and

increased

screen

time

are

associated

with

a

higher

prevalence

of

social

jetlag.

Conclusion:

The

prevalence

of

social

jetlag

was

high

in

Brazilian

adolescents,

and,

among

its

associated

factors,

studying

in

the

morning

shift

and

engaging

in

unhealthy

risk

behaviors

stand

out.

Keywords:

Social

jetlag,

Circadian

rhythm,

Sleep,

Epidemiological

studies

I
ntroduction


The

circadian

rhythm,

an

individual

biological

rhythmic

pattern,

is

susceptible

to

influences

of

biological,

genetic,

environmental,

and

behavioral

nature.
1

Changes

in

this

rhythmic

pattern

result

in

a

desynchronization

between

internal

and

external

time,

referred

to

as

social

jetlag

(SJL),

indicating

the

misalignment

of

the

biological

rhythm

caused

by

social

commitments

and

responsibilities.
1

In

adolescents,

SJL

is

more

pronounced

than

in

any

other

age

group,

primarily

due

to

bioregulatory

sleep

pressures

that

increase

nocturnal

arousal,

consequently

leading

to

a

delayed

sleep

phase.
2

Although

there

is

no

evidence

to

state

that

physiological

changes

(e.g.,

dim

light

melatonin

onset

phase)

contribute

to

phase

delay

in

mature

adolescents,
3

social

factors

play

a

significant

role.

These

include

reduced

parental

enforcement

of

bedtimes,

early

school

start

times,

academic

demands,

and

the

use

of

social

networks,

which

enhance

cognitive

arousal.

These

factors

collectively

contribute

to

the

accumulation

of

sleep

debt

during

the

week.
2

As

a

result,

adolescents

often

engage

in

weekend

catch-up

sleep

to

compensate

for

the

sleep

deficit

accrued

during

the

weekdays.
3,4

Additionally,

the

occurrence

of

SJL

in

this

age

group

is

associated

with

psychiatric

alterations,
5

increased

daytime

sleepiness,
6

shorter

sleep

duration,
7

and

cognitive

modifications

in

attention,

memory,

and

executive

function.
8,9

It

is

also

associated

with

an

alteration

in

body

mass

index

and

10,11

In

adults,

the

prevalence

of

at

least

1

hour

70%

and

students

to

30%

in

the

In

adolescents,

the

prevalence

of

SJL

can

vary

by

Among

17.8%

two

or

more

hours

as

However,

Among

In

Brazil,

few

studies

have

investigated

the

of

on

adults,

with

scarce

Therefore,

prevalent

in

female

adolescents,

older

in-

dividuals

(aged

16

to

17

years)

with

self-reported

white

skin

color,

attendees

of

private

schools,

and

with

a

higher

socioeconomic

level.

Moreover,

a

heightened

prevalence

of

SJL

is

linked

to

students

who

attend

morning

classes

and

those

who

engage

in

unhealthy

risk

behaviors,

including

skipping

breakfast,

alcohol

consumption,

and

extended

screen

time.

The

observed

prevalence

of

SJL

was

either

higher

or

similar

to

that

reported

in

other

non-Brazilian

studies.
36,37

In

the

Family

Life,

Activity,

Sun,

Health,

and

Eating

(FLASHE)

47

study,
36

which

involved

adolescents

from

all

regions

of

the

US,

observed

a

prevalence

of

SJL

of

83.2%,

with

higher

rates

among

girls

and

older

adolescents.

Moreover,

aligning

with

our

results,

Jankovic

et

al
37

noted

a

rise

in

SJL

prevalence

with

the

advancing

age

of

German

adolescents.

This

pattern

may

be

attributed

to

physical

maturation

and

the

transition

to

early

adulthood,

characterized

by

a

prolonged

wakefulness

period,

delayed

bedtime,

and

reduced

sleep

time/duration.
2

During

adolescence,

changes

are

observed

in

the

sleep/wake

homeostatic

process

mechanisms,

which

decrease,

especially

among

older

adolescents.

There

is

also

an

influence

on

the

intrinsic

rhythmic

system,

resulting

in

a

delayed

onset

of

sleep

and,

consequently,

creating

a

greater

demand

to

wake

up

later

in

the

morning.
3

The

high

prevalence

of

SJL

observed

in

the

present

study

can

be

partially

attributed

to

the

large

number

of

adolescents

enrolled

in

morning

classes

(66.8%),

as

the

class

usually

starts

at

7:30

AM

or

earlier

in

Brazil,

probably

leading

to

partial

sleep

restriction.

Additionally,

studying

in

the

morning

does

not

appear

to

prompt

adolescents

to

go

to

bed

earlier,

indicating

no

compensation

in

sleep

time

despite

the

restriction

imposed

by

classes.
38

Others

suggest

that

delaying

the

start

time

of

classes

in

this

age

group

would

increase

sleep

time,

potentially

bringing

health

benefits

and

improving

academic

performance.
36

According

to

Carrell

et

al,
39

starting

the

school

day

50

minutes

later

significantly

improves

student

achievement,

yielding

benefits

comparable

to

an

increase

in

teacher

quality.

Finally,

estimates

from

the

US

working

population

(ages

18-65)

indicate

that

circadian

misalignment

increases

healthcare

costs

by

at

least

2.3

billion

dollars

per

year

due

to

its

association

with

obesity,

diabetes,

and

cardiovascular

diseases.

Additionally,

it

can

lead

to

significant

productivity

losses.

This

highlights

how

work

schedules

and

school

start

times

can

exacerbate

the

detrimental

effects

of

circadian

rhythm

disruptions,

underscoring

the

importance

of

debating

normative

social

schedules.
40

Although

there

is

no

consensus

on

the

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

girls,

some

studies

suggest

that

girls

may

be

more

susceptible

to

the

harmful

effects

of

circadian

rhythm

misalignment.
41

This

susceptibility

may

manifest

in

increased

abdominal

fat,
36

dysregulation

of

hormones

related

to

hunger

and

satiety,
42

and

increased

insulin

resistance,

particularly

in

the

presence

of

polycystic

ovary

syndrome.
43

Regarding

skin

color,

our

results

demonstrated

a

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

adolescents

of

white

skin

color,

which

differs

from

the

study

by

Mezick

et

al,
44

who

identified

a

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

individuals

with

black

or

brown

skin

color.

This

discrepancy

may

be

attributed

to

a

greater

number

of

adolescents

identifying

themselves

as

having

white

skin

in

our

study.

Additionally,

it

is

important

to

consider

that

socioeconomic

and

environmental

characteristics

may

vary

among

different

ethnic

groups,

thereby

influencing

48

sleep

patterns

in

a

complex

manner.
45

One

associated

factor

in

another

study

was

room

temperature

variation,

which

can

impact

sleep

patterns.

In

this

study,

when

the

air

temperature

was

kept

at

a

lower

value

(25°C),

participants

experienced

colder

hands

and

feet

during

the

initial

phase

of

sleep

and

took

a

longer

time

to

fall

asleep,

consequently

reporting

poorer

sleep

quality.
46

We

observe

that

socioeconomic

factors

linked

to

higher

income

are

associated

with

a

greater

prevalence

of

SJL,

in

contrast

to

most

studies

suggesting

that

a

poorer

socioeconomic

condition

is

associated

with

a

higher

prevalence

of

sleep-related

disorders.
15

Ad-

ditionally,

a

lower

prevalence

of

SJL

was

observed

in

the

less

developed

regions

of

the

country

(North

and

Northeast).

Conversely,

regions

with

higher

economic

development

and

urbanization,

such

as

large

cities

in

Southeast

Brazil,

experience

less

exposure

to

sunlight,

more

atmospheric

and

noise

pollution,

and

increased

insecurity,

all

of

which

can

negatively

influence

individuals’

sleep

quality

and

duration.
16,47

These

results

can

also

be

partially

explained

by

geographic

location,

where

individuals

residing

at

northern

latitudes

tend

to

encounter

an

earlier

sunrise,

leading

to

earlier

engagement

in

social

activities

and

adjustments

in

their

morning

routine,
48,49

and

shorter

sleep

compared

with

those

living

in

southern

locations.
50

Further

studies

are

needed

to

investigate

the

role

of

social

and

economic

inequalities

in

adolescents’

sleep

characteristics.

Concerning

unhealthy

risk

behaviors,

adolescents

who

smoked,

drank

alcohol

and

tended

to

skip

breakfast

showed

a

higher

prevalence

of

SJL,

findings

consistent

with

the

literature.
11

Regarding

screen

exposure,

studies

indicate

that

the

use

of

smartphones

or

other

devices

emitting

blue

light,

besides

disrupting

the

sleep

cycle,

may

be

associated

with

the

development

of

cognitive

and

mood

disorders.
5

The

exposure

to

blue

light

emitted

by

screens

can

suppress

the

production

of

melatonin,

a

hormone

related

to

the

light/

dark

cycle,

delaying

the

onset

of

sleep.

It

can

also

affect

body

temperature

regulation

and

individual

perception

of

drowsiness.
51

Furthermore,

greater

cognitive

arousal

created

by

electronic

stimuli

interferes

with

the

production

of

cortisol,

leading

to

sympathetic

hyperstimulation

and

failure

to

regulate

stress.

52

Among

the

limitations

of

our

study

is

the

cross-sectional

research

design,

which

does

not

allow

for

the

establishment

of

a

causal

relationship

between

the

associated

factors

and

SJL.

The

possibility

of

reverse

causality

cannot

be

ruled

out.

The

use

of

questionnaires,

rather

than

objective

data,

to

investigate

sleep

duration

prevented

us

from

obtaining

precise

bedtime

and

wake-up

times

for

adolescents,

as

well

as

the

exact

duration

of

sleep.

The

data

acquired

represents

an

approximation

of

time

spent

in

bed,

and

it

is

prone

to

information

bias.

The

lack

of

standardization

for

the

SJL

cutoff

point

makes

it

difficult

to

compare

studies

regarding

49

prevalence

estimates.

However,

our

study

also

presents

some

strengths.

It

is

a

representative

multicenter

study

of

Brazilian

school-age

adolescents,

with

data

collected

in

a

standardized

manner,

and

the

sleep

duration

was

carefully

checked

for

consistency

in

the

reported

information.

The

large

sample

size

allowed

us

to

analyze

the

prevalence

of

SJL

according

to

different

covariates.

Finally,

the

presented

SJL

prevalence

estimates

provide

novel

information

for

many

regions

in

Brazil.

Conclusion

The

results

of

this

study

are

of

a

high

prevalence

of

SJL

among

Brazilian

school-age

adolescents,

especially

among

older

individuals,

females,

those

of

white

ethnicity,

those

attending

private

schools,

and

those

with

higher

socioeconomic

status.

The

higher

prevalence

of

SJL

in

students

of

the

morning

shift,

along

with

an

earlier

start

time

for

classes,

suggests

a

potential

partial

sleep

restriction,

indicating

that

modifications

of

school

schedules

could

be

beneficial.

Intervention

studies

to

decrease

the

duration

of

SJL

and

follow-ups

aimed

at

investigating

the

impact

of

SJL

on

health

outcomes

and

academic

performance

are

essential

for

a

comprehensive

understanding

of

their

role

throughout

the

lifespan.
